summary: A description of how to use Harvard's PDP-10 program for network remote job entry, which at that time worked only with UCLA. A user starts the program, opens a Telnet connection to UCLA for commands, and uses FTP-style commands to submit jobs and get results.

plainLanguage.summary: A how-to for using one university's program to send jobs to another university's computer and pick up the results.

questions: submitting jobs to ucla over arpanet
subtitle: Harvard's PDP-10 program for submitting jobs to UCLA over the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: Researchers at Harvard wanted to use UCLA's faster computer for computationally intensive work but needed a way to submit jobs and retrieve results over the network.
tldr.mechanism: Harvard developed an RJE (Remote Job Entry) program running on its PDP-10 that opens a Telnet connection to UCLA for commands and an FTP data connection for transferring job input and output. Users run RJE locally and issue commands to control submission, retrieval, and job status.
tldr.outcome: Harvard users could run jobs at UCLA almost as if they were physically present, with local commands translating to UCLA's RJS protocol. The system supported job routing, queue management, and various output control options.

today: RFC 499 describes a 1973 remote job entry system. The concepts of command and data channels, queue management, and network-based job submission influenced the design of modern distributed computing and grid systems.

sections.title: Remote Job Entry over the Network
sections.content: RFC 499 describes Harvard's RJE program, which allows users to submit jobs to UCLA-CCN's IBM 360/91 from Harvard's PDP-10 over the ARPA Network. The program establishes two connections: a Telnet connection for commands and control, and an FTP connection for transferring job input and output data. Users must arrange an account and password at UCLA beforehand. The program translates local commands into UCLA's RJS protocol, allowing Harvard users to work with UCLA's resources without learning UCLA's native interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A Harvard program talks to UCLA's computer through two connections: one for commands and one for sending and getting data.

sections.title: Local and Remote Commands
sections.content: Users start RJE at monitor level and open a Telnet connection to UCLA with the command RJE UCL. Local commands (prefixed with an asterisk) are processed by Harvard: *READ sends a file of job cards formatted for UCLA, *PRINT retrieves print output from UCLA's printer and reformats it for Harvard's line printer, and *QUIT tears down all connections. Remote commands (no prefix) are sent to UCLA's RJS and control job submission, status checking, queue management, and output routing. A user must understand both systems: the local (Harvard) command processor and the foreign (UCLA) RJS processor.
sections.plainLanguage: You type commands starting with * to control Harvard's side (read files, print output, quit), and regular commands to control UCLA's side (signon, run jobs, check status).

sections.title: Job Management and Output Handling
sections.content: UCLA's RJS distinguishes between Active and Deferred output queues. When a user opens the print or punch channel via *PRINT, output from the Active Queue is sent immediately. Deferred output must be explicitly requested by job name using the RESET command. The SET command allows users to change the VRBT (virtual remote batch terminal) properties, such as the default output destination and deferral status. Other commands include DEFER (move output to deferred queue), ROUTE (redirect output to another terminal), ABORT (cancel a job), and output stream controls like BSP (backspace), CAN (cancel), RST (restart), and REPEAT (extra copies).
sections.plainLanguage: Jobs can be queued as ready-to-pick-up (Active) or waiting-for-request (Deferred), and many commands let you manage where output goes and what to do with it.
